title: Staff training pilot
scenario: An internal learning team plans a small onboarding pilot, clarifies optional participation, and separates feedback gathering from employee assessment.
transcript:
[00:00] Rowan: The purpose today is to plan the pilot of our new project-handoff training. We are testing the training materials, not rating staff performance. I want that distinction in the invitation and in the facilitator notes, because the word assessment in the draft could easily suggest something else.
[00:26] Sasha: I used assessment to mean a short exercise at the end, but I see the problem. The exercise asks people to read a fictional handoff and identify missing information. It is not connected to any personnel record, and there is no pass mark. I can rename it practice activity.
[00:53] Luis: That would help. I would also avoid collecting named scores. We can learn whether the example is clear by asking which parts of the instructions people had to reread. If someone misses a detail, that may tell us about the exercise wording rather than their ability to do their job.
[01:20] Mei: For logistics, the training room is available Wednesday morning. The draft invitation says everyone on the operations team is required to attend, but I thought we wanted a small volunteer group first. I have not sent the invitation because those two descriptions do not match.
[01:45] Rowan: Thank you for holding it. This is an optional pilot with six volunteers, not mandatory training for the whole team. We are not announcing a company-wide rollout. If fewer than six people are available, we can still run it; we do not need to pressure anyone to fill the seats.
[02:12] Sasha: I planned forty-five minutes: ten for the introduction, fifteen for the example, fifteen for discussion, and five for feedback. That may be too much talking in the introduction. I can move the background explanation into a short pre-read, but I do not want attendance to depend on reading it in advance.
[02:40] Luis: Could the pre-read be optional, with a concise recap at the start? Some people will prefer having the outline early; others will arrive without preparation time. The activity should include everything needed to participate. We can ask afterward whether the advance outline was useful without treating it as homework.
[03:07] Rowan: Yes. Send an optional one-page outline and include the essential context in the session. Keep the whole pilot to forty-five minutes. I would rather reduce the introduction than remove the feedback period, because the pilot is supposed to tell us what to change before a broader use.
[03:33] Mei: Wednesday morning contains two possible slots, nine and eleven. Which should I offer? I cannot hold both indefinitely because another team asked for the room. We have not checked the volunteers' availability yet, so choosing now might exclude the people who want to help.
[03:58] Rowan: Offer both slots in the availability question today and close responses Monday at noon. Mei, please choose the better-attended slot after that and release the other room hold. We can state Wednesday as the proposed day, but the exact session time is not decided in this meeting.
[04:24] Sasha: I have a content question about the fictional handoff. It includes an urgent request with no deadline, a task assigned to two people, and a document link without access instructions. Are those too many issues in one example? I do not want the exercise to feel like a trick.
[04:51] Luis: Three is manageable if we tell people the aim is to notice missing information, not guess what the sender meant. We should allow answers like ask who owns this or deadline not stated. The model answer should not invent a deadline just to make the handoff look complete.
[05:18] Rowan: Keep those three issues. In the discussion, separate identifying a gap from resolving it. A reader cannot determine an unstated owner by confidence or seniority. That is a central lesson of the training, and the facilitator should demonstrate asking a clear follow-up question.
[05:42] Mei: Do we need laptops? If people need to access the shared document, I should mention that. But printed copies may make it easier to look at the example while listening, and it would reduce the risk of someone spending the first ten minutes dealing with account access.
[06:08] Sasha: Let us provide printed copies and an accessible text version beforehand. A laptop will be optional. People can mark the printed example, type notes, or simply discuss it. The feedback questions should not depend on how they chose to take part.
[06:31] Luis: For feedback, I suggest three questions: what was clear, what required another explanation, and what would help you use the handoff checklist later. We can make names optional. I do not need a numerical satisfaction score for such a small pilot, especially if it hides the specific changes people suggest.
[06:58] Rowan: Agreed on those three questions and optional names. Do not ask participants to describe personal health or learning conditions to explain their preferences. Practical feedback about format, pace, and wording is enough for this purpose. We can act on it without assigning labels to anyone.
[07:23] Mei: I will set up the availability form today and the feedback form once Luis sends the wording. Does the invitation come from me or from the team managers? If it comes from a manager, the word optional may feel less convincing even if it is written clearly.
[07:49] Rowan: Send it from the learning team account through the usual process. I will tell managers that participation is voluntary and that they should not nominate people as a performance intervention. That message is my responsibility today. We are asking for help improving a draft resource.
[08:14] Sasha: I can finish the practice activity and optional outline by Friday afternoon. I originally offered Thursday, but I need Friday because I am revising the answer guide as well. Please record Friday as the final deadline so nobody waits for a version I am no longer promising tomorrow.
[08:41] Luis: I will send the three feedback questions tomorrow morning and review Sasha's answer guide Monday afternoon. My review will check whether it distinguishes stated facts from assumptions. It will not be a complete review of every training resource the team uses.
[09:04] Mei: Once the slot is selected Monday, I will send the final invitation with the participant time, optional outline, and note that laptops are not required. I will keep the two tentative holds until the response deadline, then release the unused one as agreed.
[09:28] Rowan: To close: optional six-person pilot, forty-five minutes, one fictional handoff, several ways to participate, and descriptive feedback. The exact Wednesday time and any wider rollout remain undecided. We have not approved a recording of the session. Please keep recording out of the invitation unless we discuss it separately.
[09:55] Sasha: That is clear. I will label the materials as a pilot and remove the assessment language. We will learn from what people say about the materials, without turning the practice activity into a score. Thanks; I have enough direction to finish the draft.
